steps.label: Kickoff & Game Analysis
steps.summary: Season begins with full game analysis — every scoring element, every rule, every strategic constraint.
steps.detail: At kickoff, the team watches the game release and immediately breaks down the field. Every scoring element is catalogued with its point value and estimated difficulty. The output feeds directly into the Game Points Matrix: a structured ranking of what the robot should pursue, in what order, and why. No design decisions are made until this baseline exists.

steps.label: Strategy & Simulation
steps.summary: Game Points Matrix + Monte Carlo simulation — predict score ranges and mission times before building anything.
steps.detail: The Game Points Matrix compares each task's scoring value against implementation difficulty, producing a prioritized list of capabilities. That list feeds a custom Excel-based Monte Carlo simulation — 50+ simulated games per iteration — which projects expected score ranges and mission times under realistic conditions. This tells the team whether a proposed design is viable before a single part is cut.

steps.label: Design & Trade-offs
steps.summary: CAD-first design with cost/benefit analysis at every fork — trade-offs are documented, not guessed.
steps.detail: Every design decision is evaluated with cost/benefit analysis: weight, complexity, reliability, and fabrication time weighed against expected performance gain. Multiple concepts are explored in Onshape before anything is fabricated. The DHF structure requires that each design decision is traceable — if a choice is made, there is a documented reason. 100% of the robot is designed in CAD before manufacturing begins.

steps.label: Fabricate
steps.summary: Custom fabrication — CNC milling and 3D printing — from CAD to physical parts.
steps.detail: Nearly every robot part is custom-fabricated using the team's three CNC mills (custom MPCNC, 6"×6" industrial mill, large PrintNC) and 3D printers. The CAD-first workflow means parts are cut to spec, not iterated by hand. Subsystems are assembled and bench-tested independently before integration, following the DHF subsystem-based design requirement.

steps.label: Test & Iterate (FMEA)
steps.summary: FMEA surfaces failure modes before competition. Every failure is documented, root-caused, and fixed.
steps.detail: Failure Mode and Effect Analysis (FMEA) is applied systematically: every subsystem is evaluated for potential failure modes, their likelihood, and their impact on match performance. Observed failures during testing are logged, prioritized by severity, and assigned to sprint tasks. Monte Carlo runs are updated with new timing data after each test session. This loop — test, observe, FMEA, fix, re-simulate — repeats across the 8-month season.

steps.label: Competition-Ready
steps.summary: Data-verified, mechanically proven, and strategically tuned — the robot earns its place on the field.
steps.detail: Before each competition, the team reviews the Game Points Matrix against current robot capabilities, runs a final Monte Carlo pass with observed match performance data, and confirms all FMEA items are resolved or mitigated. Post-match analysis feeds back into the sprint cycle for the next event. The process doesn't end at competition — it closes the loop for the next iteration.

dhf.summary: A GE Healthcare engineering framework used to develop FDA-regulated medical devices — applied here to FTC robotics.
dhf.question: Design History File — the GE Healthcare origin
bullets: Framework comes directly from GE Healthcare's medical device development process
Used in production of FDA-regulated hardware: MRI machines, CT scanners, X-ray systems
Team coaches are CTOs at GE Healthcare — they introduced the process to the team
Core principle: every design decision is documented, traceable, and reviewable

dhf.summary: The team's shorthand: Define · Hypothesize · Fabricate maps the industrial framework onto the FTC season.
dhf.question: Define · Hypothesize · Fabricate — the team's reading
bullets: Define — game breakdown, scoring priorities, robot requirements, and constraints
Hypothesize — design concepts, simulation runs, cost/benefit analysis, CAD models
Fabricate — custom manufacturing, subsystem testing, FMEA, and iteration
Three phases mirror the FTC season timeline, making the framework student-actionable

dhf.summary: Every subsystem is designed, built, and validated in isolation before it touches the rest of the robot.
dhf.question: Subsystem-based design
bullets: Each robot subsystem is scoped, designed, and tested as an independent unit
Integration only happens after individual subsystem tests pass
Isolates failure points — a broken mechanism doesn't halt the whole build
Matches GE Healthcare's medical-device validation methodology

dhf.summary: Every specification links back to a documented design goal — nothing is built without a recorded reason.
dhf.question: Requirement traceability
bullets: Each design requirement traces to a scoring goal from the Game Points Matrix
Design decisions are logged with rationale, not just outcomes
Enables post-match review: if performance misses a target, the trace shows why
Mirrors FDA traceability requirements applied to life-critical hardware

dhf.summary: No fabrication before CAD review. No integration before subsystem test. Gates enforce quality at every transition.
dhf.question: Formal design review gates
bullets: CAD review gate: 100% of parts modeled in Onshape before any manufacturing begins
Subsystem gate: bench-test results must pass before the part joins the full robot
Integration gate: full robot assembly only after all subsystem gates are cleared
Gates are team-enforced checkpoints, not suggestions — they match industrial review cadence
